subject: Climate & Environment
title: Deep Sea Mining
description: A 60-second lesson on Deep Sea Mining.

hook.text: The deep ocean floor holds trillions of dollars in metals. Companies want to mine it.

buildup.text: Polymetallic nodules on the seafloor contain manganese, cobalt, nickel — all needed for batteries.

discovery.text: Mining would vacuum the ocean floor, destroying habitats that took millions of years to form.

twist.text: Deep-sea ecosystems are barely explored. We may destroy species before we discover them.

climax.text: Over 30 countries have called for a moratorium. The debate is intensifying.

punchline.text: We're about to mine a world we don't even understand yet.

quiz.question: What are polymetallic nodules?
options: Metal-rich rocks on the deep ocean floor

details.summary: Deep-sea mining targets mineral-rich nodules, crusts, and hydrothermal vents on the ocean floor that contain metals like manganese, cobalt, and nickel needed for batteries and electronics. Scientists warn that mining could destroy fragile deep-sea ecosystems that take centuries to recover.
details.whyItMatters: Demand for battery metals is surging with the energy transition. Whether deep-sea mining proceeds or is banned will set a precedent for how humanity balances resource needs with ocean conservation.
takeaways: The deep seafloor holds vast deposits of battery metals
Mining could devastate slow-growing deep-sea ecosystems
Regulations are still being debated internationally

faq.question: What minerals are targeted by deep-sea mining?
faq.answer: Primary targets are polymetallic nodules rich in manganese, nickel, cobalt, and copper. Seafloor massive sulfides near hydrothermal vents contain gold, silver, and zinc. Cobalt-rich crusts on seamounts are also coveted for battery production.

faq.question: Why are scientists concerned about deep-sea mining?
faq.answer: Deep-sea ecosystems grow extremely slowly; nodule fields take millions of years to form. Mining would destroy habitats, create sediment plumes that smother organisms over wide areas, and remove species we have barely begun to catalog.
